name: AMT49413GEVATR
title: AMT49413: three-phase BLDC controller and N-channel MOSFET gate driver
summary: A controller for three-phase brushless DC motors with Hall sensors that drives six external N-channel MOSFETs. It decodes the Hall signals, sets dead time with one resistor, regulates the motor current with a fixed-frequency PWM loop and a gain-19 sense amplifier, and accepts an external PWM. A charge pump makes the 13 V gate supply, bootstrap capacitors with top-off pumps drive the high sides up to 100% duty, and short, undervoltage, overtemperature, Hall and low-load faults are reported on two flags. It runs from 5.5 to 50 V in a 7 × 7 mm 48-pin QFN.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The controller runs a three-phase N-channel MOSFET bridge from VBAT+ for a BLDC motor with Hall sensors. Each phase has a high-side FET (gate on GHx, source on Sx) and a low-side FET (gate on GLx), with a bootstrap capacitor from Cx to Sx feeding the floating high-side driver. One pump capacitor sits across CP1 and CP2. The low-side sources join at LSS and CSP and return to ground through the sense resistor, whose ground end goes to CSN and AGND. The three Hall outputs go to H1 to H3; Direction drives DIR and the Current Limit voltage drives REF.

parts.value: 3-phase BLDC motor with three Hall sensors

notes: Run/Stop drives one of U1's logic inputs.

circuits.title: Supply and ground connections
circuits.description: The bridge, its supply and the controller's own parts arranged for a clean ground. VBB and VDRAIN both come from the + Supply rail, VDRAIN tapping it at the high-side drains. Gate resistors sit in series with all six gates. The low-side sources join LSS and return to Supply Common through RSENSE, the power ground. VBB, VREG and V5 capacitors go to a controller supply ground; the VDSTH divider from V5, RT and CT on RC, and RDEAD go to a quiet ground. Both grounds meet at AGND, which runs on its own trace to Supply Common at one point. A zener and diode in series, and a capacitor, between LSS and AGND are optional clamps for LSS transients. Two capacitors bypass the bridge supply.

operation.text: The chip commutates and current-limits a three-phase BLDC motor with Hall sensors through an external N-channel MOSFET bridge, using fixed-frequency PWM. It decodes the three Hall signals, keeps the two FETs of a leg from conducting together, and has separate DIR, BRAKE and COAST controls. A sense resistor in the bridge ground return is amplified and compared with REF to limit the current cycle by cycle; an external PWM signal can control the bridge instead, with the internal loop off or setting a ceiling.

All internal circuits run from integrated regulators, so VBB is the only supply; it is fed through reverse-battery protection. Gate drive stays above 10 V on both sides down to VBB = 7 V; from 7 V to 5.5 V the part still works with less gate drive.

V5 comes from a regulator controller driving an external NPN, QV5: V5BD gives the base current and V5 senses the output. It also powers the internal logic. V5 needs at least 200 nF to AGND and V5BD 100 nF to AGND. When V5 with QV5 also powers other circuits, put 10 µF from V5 to AGND close to the pins (with 100 nF ceramic in parallel if electrolytic). Without QV5, join V5 to V5BD and decouple with at least 220 nF.

A charge pump with a capacitor across CP1 and CP2 (470 nF typical) makes VREG, 13 V nominal, which powers all six drivers and charges the bootstrap capacitors. It doubles at low supply and drops out at the nominal 14 V to keep its dissipation down. The VREG capacitor carries the low-side gate transients: at least 20 times the bootstrap capacitor, low ESR and ESL, X7R ceramic at best, or an electrolytic with about 100 nF ceramic beside it, placed at the pin with its ground near AGND.

Each high-side driver floats on its Sx pin and is supplied from a bootstrap capacitor on Cx, charged to about VREG while Sx is low. A trickle top-off charge pump per phase (under 100 µA typical) replaces the floating circuit's bias draw (under 20 µA), so a high-side FET can stay on indefinitely (100% duty). The charge to first turn a gate on always comes from the bootstrap capacitor.

H1 to H3 expect sensors 120 electrical degrees apart; 60° sensors work with an external inverter. Open-collector sensors need pull-ups to 5 V, which V5 can supply. The inputs have about 500 mV hysteresis and a filter, and each is pulled up internally through 100 kΩ and a diode, so a missing sensor reads high. All three at the same level is a logic fault. A microcontroller can drive the inputs directly.

GHx and GLx source current from their upper (PMOS) half when at 1 and sink from their lower (NMOS) half when at 0; GHx sinks into Sx, GLx into LSS. Series gate resistors near each FET gate set the slew rate and with it the current and voltage slew at the phase node. Sx and LSS carry the gate discharge currents and need low-impedance traces to the bridge.

A dead time between one FET turning off and its partner turning on is set by RDEAD to AGND, from 96 ns to 6.3 µs; RDEAD open or tied to V5 gives about 6 µs. It must cover the spread in MOSFET gate capacitance and in the gate resistance inside and outside the chip.

RESET low shuts every internal circuit down, V5 included. On wake the gate outputs are held off until the charge pump is up, about 3 ms in normal conditions. RESET has a 50 kΩ pull-down and a 6 V clamp; to start without a logic signal a resistor of more than 20 kΩ to the battery can hold it high, small enough still to reach the RESET high threshold.

COAST low turns every FET off with the supplies and logic still running. BRAKE low turns all low-side FETs on and high-side FETs off, shorting the windings' back EMF; the braking torque depends on speed and the winding current is not controlled. RESET low or COAST low overrides BRAKE. MODE high selects slow decay (only the high-side FET switches off in the PWM off-time, low ripple, slower response, suited to near-constant speed); MODE low selects fast decay (both FETs switch, quicker response, more ripple, suited to start-stop and positioning). DIR sets the torque direction; with a high-inertia load and fast decay, reversing DIR brakes the motor.

The sense amplifier output is compared with REF; at the trip point the source driver is latched off and the current recirculates, in the path MODE selects, until the next PWM period. With PWM held high, torque follows the REF voltage. REF clamps at 4 V internally, so a resistor RREF of 20 to 200 kΩ to V5 sets the maximum without an external reference. CSOUT is also available for an external loop.

RT and CT in parallel from RC to AGND set the internal oscillator. Pulling RC to AGND stops the oscillator and holds the PWM latch on, for purely external PWM; current is then not limited by the chip, though short detection still works and an external loop using CSOUT must blank the switching transients itself. With both in use the internal frequency is set below the external one: PWM low discharges CT, so the external signal synchronises the internal circuit and dead time, the comparator and blanking all stay active. The PWM frequency should be above the audible range and low enough for the bootstrap capacitor to charge.

When a source driver turns on, recovery currents of the body diodes and load capacitance cause a spike; the current comparator is ignored for tBLANK, set by CT, so the spike does not trip it. CT must be large enough to cover the spike. The blank masks only the internal comparator.

Too large a bootstrap capacitor wastes charging time and limits duty cycle and PWM frequency; too small one droops when its charge moves to the gate. QBOOT about 20 times QGATE is used. The capacitor charges through the internal bootstrap diode from VREG whenever Sx is pulled low by a GLx cycle.

Each phase's bootstrap voltage is watched against VBOOTUV. If it falls below, the chip turns on that phase's low-side FET until the voltage exceeds VBOOTUV plus its hysteresis; charging takes at least 7 µs typically, longer for CBOOT above 1000 nF. If the threshold is not reached within about 200 µs an undervoltage fault is flagged.

During the PWM off-time the chip turns on the FET that MODE selects so the recirculating current flows in the channel, not the body diode; the diodes conduct only during dead time. With internal current control in fast decay, synchronous rectification turns off at zero current so the current does not reverse. With external PWM in fast decay, the current is allowed to rise in reverse to the set limit before synchronous rectification is disabled.

Brake current does not pass through RSENSE, so the FET ratings must be checked. A PWM signal on BRAKE can limit braking current, its duty found for each condition, typically starting at a current-limiting value and falling to 0% (BRAKE held low) to hold the motor still. With RESET = 1, COAST = 0 takes priority over BRAKE: every bridge FET goes off and the motor freewheels.

A brush DC motor can be driven as a full bridge by fixing the Hall inputs to one state and leaving the phase that state makes high-impedance unconnected: with H1 = H2 = 1 and H3 = 0, CC, GHC, SC and GLC float. DIR then sets rotation and PWM and MODE set the current behaviour.

TACHO changes state at every commutation point in either direction. DIRO is updated at each commutation: high for forward (the Hall sequence running down the commutation table), low for reverse (running up). DIRO can differ from DIR, for example while a high-inertia load is being braked after DIR is reversed; it does not change during that braking.

Two open-drain flags, FF1 and FF2, code the fault per the fault action table; with several faults at once each flag is the AND of the fault states. With ESF = 1 a short fault turns all gate drives off and coasts the motor, latched until the next commutation or COAST or RESET goes low, so a running motor coasts safely to the next commutation. With ESF = 0 the flags still assert but the bridge keeps running and is not protected; the host must act, by RESET or COAST. Tying FF1 and FF2 to COAST with a pull-up to V5 gives a simple disable.

During power-up both flags are pulled low and the motor coasts until VREG exceeds about 8 V. That is enough to turn the FETs on at a 5.5 V battery but not to reach their rated on-resistance, which can overheat them. The bootstrap voltage and V5 are monitored too; either below its lockout sets the flags.
Overtemperature pulls both flags low and disables nothing; turning the part off is left to the system.

All three Hall inputs equal is an illegal code: both flags go low and the motor coasts. The fault is not latched, so the FETs are driven again per the commutation table once the inputs are valid. The pull-ups make an open sensor wire show as this fault.

Short to ground: the voltage across each high-side FET (VDRAIN minus Sx) is compared with VDSTH. Short to supply: the voltage across each low-side FET (Sx minus LSS) is compared with VDSTH. A shorted winding is seen across both FETs of a phase. Each pulls FF2 low. The voltages are sampled only one dead time after a FET turns on, to ignore motor capacitance. With ESF = 0 the internal current limit gives little or no protection, above all when a phase is shorted to ground.

If the sense amplifier output stays below VCSOL through a commutation period, FF1 goes low and nothing else happens; an open phase may still let a running motor turn at reduced performance. The flag is set at the next commutation and cleared after a later period without the fault. After start-up or reset it stays set until the current first exceeds VCSOL, so an open phase is seen even if the motor cannot start. A motor with no mechanical load can also trip it.
VBB: at least 100 nF ceramic to AGND, with about 10 µF electrolytic in parallel. Every supply pin's capacitor goes close to its pin.

AGND is the single ground pin and carries only the controller's current; FET gate currents return elsewhere. It is the reference for the current trip, the VDS threshold and the timing parts and must stay quiet. RDEAD and VDSTH parts go to a quiet ground taken straight to AGND, never to supply common or power ground. VBB, VREG and V5 decoupling go to a controller supply ground joined near AGND. Timing parts may use either, not power ground. The exposed pad ties to AGND. With little room the two may be combined if RDEAD's return is close to AGND. AGND runs on its own low-impedance trace to supply common at one point.

Keep GHx, GLx, Sx and LSS traces short. Run LSS on its own trace to the bridge common, not to AGND, and not shared with CSP. Route CSP and CSN as separate, matched traces. Use short wide copper at all power FET drains and sources, motor leads and supply bus. 100 nF ceramic across each FET's drain and source can limit spikes. Check LSS transients against AGND with a short-ground probe; if they pass the absolute maximum, add clamping, capacitance or both between LSS and AGND. Tie TEST to AGND. VDRAIN is a Kelvin trace from the high-side drains.
At high ambient temperature the chip's own dissipation, estimated with the power equations, must keep the junction in its safe range.
